image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   A **faceted bar chart** (small multiples of vertical bar charts).

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - Uses **faceting / small multiples** in a **2×2 grid**.  
   - Each panel shows one setting where people make friends:
     - In high school
     - In college
     - At work
     - In the neighborhood
   - Bars are **not stacked**; color is used to highlight bars relative to an average reference line.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Place where people make friends (high school / college / work / neighborhood) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel titles |
| Income rank | Ordinal | Position on x-axis; ordered bars from 5th to 100th percentile |
| Relative likelihood / rate compared with average | Quantitative | Bar height / position on y-axis |
| Above/below average status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of bars (dark vs light) relative to the dashed “AVG.” line |
| Average reference | Quantitative | Horizontal dashed reference line; text label “AVG.” |
| Selected annotated values (e.g., 0.9x, 0.3x, 1.9x, 2.4x) | Quantitative | Text labels/annotations |

comments.raw_comment:
The graphs are talking about levels of income and where people are likely to make friends. The x-axis includes what percentile of income they’re in. People who were in a higher income percentile tended to make more friends in college than people in the lower income percentile. People in the middle percentile tended to make friends at work or in high school. People in the lower percentiles tended to make friends from their neighborhoods. The main thing I wonder if why high school seems to be just a flat line. Why do people from all areas tend to make some friends there? Is it because high school is a thing most people attend? Talking about wealth is something important for our community especially. Eden Prairie has a very diverse mix of incomes, especially in our high school. Though the majority of students' families make a pretty good wage, there are still plenty who don’t have a very high income or have an extremely high income. It’s good to look at where everyone is coming from and how their lives differ and use that to reflect on ourselves. 
How The Different Incomes Form Friendships

If I were to create a catchy headline for this it would be: How likely are YOU to make friends?

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that wealthier students make more friends in college, making the graph skew to the left. The number of wealthy college students making friends highly exceeds the number of lower-class students doing to the same. I also noticed that in neighborhoods, kids with families that have lower incomes make more connections than those in neighborhoods with higher income, skewing the graph to the right. The in-school and at-work graphs show that making friends in those places don't depend on your income. 

I wonder if wealthy students make more friends during college because they dont have to necessarily worry about paying for their college. In the meantime, the lower-income students most likely depend on jobs and work and dont have time to make more friends. Also, kids in a lower income neighborhood probably form connections based on the similar lifestyles they live while wealthier neighborhoods are probably more isolated. 

This relates to me and my community because I live in a middle income neighborhood, and it is surprising to see that how much money your family and those around you make dictates the kind of friendships you will form.

A catchy title for this graph could be "More money more friends? Family incomes surprisingly impact social connections."

Additionally, both lower and higher income individuals make friends in high school and at work hence the approximately normal distributed graph.

What I wonder is that are the friendships made in high school/at work more genuine and long lasting compared to the one in college or the neighborhood? The graphs show that both high income and low income people mutually made their friends in high school or work while the other two graphs are skewed.

This relates to my community as a high school student. The graph of people making friends in high school is almost normally distributed, meaning that the students are friends no matter their income. I believe that this is accurate, as me and most of the people I know don’t base friendships on money but more on similar interests on media, sports, hobbies, etc.

An interesting title for this graph can be “Money for Companionships”.

What do you notice? I notice that graphs for in high school and at work have a similar shape and have a peak near the center, indicating that most friends were made among people with a middle/average income. Most people making friends in the neighborhood are those that lower come and it is 1.9 times more likely than the average.

What do you wonder? I wonder why as a society we are allowing income to determine the relationships or friendships that are made. I wonder if it has to do with the different opportunities that rise in college and neighborhoods, given that there is less of a common goal. Schools have a main goal of graduating and in a working environment to get a paycheck. Meanwhile most people have a different goal in college and neighborhoods.

How does this relate to me and my community? This relates to me because I am a senior in high school so I relate to the high school graph. From my personal experience, I have made friends and will continue to make friends with people of all income levels. I have noticed most if not all my peers do the same when it comes to making friends. I think a lot of this has to do with the fact that we all share similar incomes.

This relates to me and my community because I am in high school and it is interesting to see how income becomes a factor in social standing as you get into college.

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that the reason high school may be so small is because the audience answering the question is between the ages of 25 and 44. Memory deteriorates over time, and it would make sense that in this case, the high school experience would be forgotten. However, it makes me think of how brief high school is and how friends wait in other places.
I inferred that college friends come from money. If one is barely scraping by and is using in their resources to arrive at the highest potential, they will study and attend classes, focusing. Americans who have enough money will be more likely to attend secondary institutes. No one in college has enough money, but there is an abundance of friends.
As far as work friends go, they seem to come from where one falls in the workplace food chain. If you are in manual labor, you won’t be talking to those in ranks above you, and if you are a director or coordinator, you won’t be stopping by everyone’s offices checking in. I can assume that, if the graph went further, the symmetry would not change, rather, it could follow the trend. 
And finally, in the neighborhood, those who don’t have much in the material sense have the most in companionship. Those who live so close to each other, are usually roughly in the same boat, and have nothing to prove to those around them, making more friends in the long run.

If I were to name this graph, I would have it titled something along the lines of “Proof That Friends Are More Important Than Money”.

1) What do you notice?
I noticed that that relationship between income and friends varies a lot from place to place. In high school, the central 50% /average income makes slightly more friends than the average. This graph had a more significant upwards/positive curve then the previous, showing how much more weight a higher income holds in college than in high school, where presumably less people have their own income. Then at work, the graph more closely resembles that of highschool, probably because you're usually surrounded by people making around the same as you. In the neighborhood, the graph was also curved but now in a negative way, the lowest 25th percentile being 1.9x more likely than average to make friends.

I wonder how the statistics vary when you view whether people of different incomes make more or less friends in general?
3) How does this relate to you and your community?
Coming from a lower income community, this graph is relatable because it shows how people with lower incomes are more likely to befriend one another then people with higher incomes- probably due to the heightened sense of community those who make less tend to foster.
4) What’s going on in this graph?
My title would be "Does Money Buy Friends?"

comments.raw_comment:
1. I noticed that people making friends in high school and at work are very similar in shape. Making friends in college and in the neighborhood are opposite of each other. In high school, the graph seems to be roughly symmetrical which means that whether one comes from higher or lower income, there is no difference in the amount of friends. I also notice that it is 0.5x more likely than average for higher income people to make friends in college than lower income people in their neighborhoods. 
2. I wonder if lower income people make less friends in college because they might feel inferior to those who come from upper class. I also wonder if high income people make less friends in their neighborhood because they probably live in towns where the houses are very separated and they aren't able to build connections. I'm curious if in college higher income people make more friends just because they are wealthy and other people seem them as a way to get opportunities because networking is important. 
3.This is relevant to me and my community because coming from a low income area, I do believe that lower income people make more friends from their neighborhood because most of us live very close together and grew up in the same schools. In my high school, there are also some people that are upper class but income doesn't affect the way they make friends because no one really cares at our age how much money our families have. 
4. Friends For The Money or Loyalty?

comments.raw_comment:
In high school, I see that people generally make friends no matter their income. In college, people make an exponentially higher amount of friends, almost 2.5 times the average, when they have a higher income. I am curious whether this is because having a job in college exposes people to more opportunities to make friends. In neighborhoods, people who make less money make more friends. The lowest level of income has more than twice the average number of friends. In the workplace, more friends are likely with average pay than a higher or lower income. 
I wonder mostly why income is being compared to friends and if the two are realistically related. I am also curious if people make more friends in their neighborhood when they have a lower income because they have more time for socialization. I also wonder how income was compared in high school students and if people who make no money are considered. 
This graph relates to me because as a high school student, it makes sense that people of all incomes make friends. People are not judged based on whether they have a job or not. 
A title for this graph would be "What does it cost to make a friend?"

This relates to me because I am about to start the next phase of my life in college and it is interesting to know the chances of making friends in college or in a neighborhood setting. It is relevant to my community because where friends are made is heavily tied to current issues like accessibility, transportation, and available time outside of work and school.

In “At work,” this difference is more pronounced, with the middle-income percentile making the highest percentage of friends in the workplace. In the “In college” graph, it is clear that those with a higher income make a larger percentage of their friends in college. Those with a lower income make a higher percentage of their friends “In the neighborhood” than other social places. One potential headline could be “The Real Fortune: Friends and Finances”.

comments.raw_comment:
The graph represents the likelihood of people to make friends in different locations depending on their income. The blue portions of the bars represent those who make more friends than average in that location.

I wonder how the answers would have changed if they were to poll a larger age demographic than just people between the ages of 25 to 44.

I observe that across all of the income levels people tend to make friends in high school. The is likely because high school is a universal experience, relatively independent of income. It is similar for the work graph. The middle class (30th-80th) percentiles make the most friends at work. The friendship levels at college showcase more of a stark difference. The upper wealth classes (60th-100th) are well above average in making friends in college. This is due to the fact that college is very expensive, meaning that it would be the foremost place for wealthy people to make friends. The opposite is true for the neighborhood. Those in the lowest income levels report making the most friends in this location.

This relates to me and my community in the sense that I am currently in high school, where friendship is equal across income levels. However, it is necessary to understand the ways that income can affect all areas of our lives. Through analyzing this graph we can gain insights into our society, such as the inaccessibility of college for lower income levels.

Friendship According to Income: Can Money Truly Buy Friends?

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, Feb. 10 with moderation on Wednesday, Feb. 15.  The topic – human population over the past 11,700 years.

comments.raw_comment: I notice that for students in high school, income rank does not play a huge role in making friends because the graph is uniform. There is a slight increase around the middle 50% of income and slight dips at both extremes. This is similar to the graph of those making friends at work. This could be because people in high schools don't necessarily care much about their classmates' income, and they make friends with them based on who they are instead of how much they make. Similarly, it is possible that those that work together may not care as much about how much their colleague makes because they all work in the same environment. I also notice that income plays a role in making friends in college and neighborhoods. In college, people who. make a higher income are 2.4x more likely to make friends, while in the neighborhood, it's the reverse; people who make a lower income are 1.9x as likely to make friends. I wonder why this is. Is it because people in college want to go on experiences and trips, so they become friends with people who make more money? Do people with a lower income make friends in neighborhoods because they come across as more relatable and less intimidating or snobbish? This relates to me because I don't consider income to be a main factor in making friends, but it makes me wonder if people around me do. My headline is "Rags or Riches: How income plays a role in making friends."

What do you notice? 
I notice that in high school, people with middle income are more likely to make friends, but not by much. In college, people with higher incomes are 2.4 times more likely to make friends than the average person. At work, people with a middle income are more likely to make friends. In the neighborhood, people with a lower income are 1.9 times more likely to make friends than the average person. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why people with middle income do not have a certain place where they make friends, whereas people with high and low incomes have different places where they are more likely to make friends. In addition, I wonder why people with a higher income are more likely to make friends in college and why people with a lower income are more likely to make friends in their neighborhoods. 

How does this relate to you and your community? 
This relates to my community because it shows where people are more likely to make friends. In addition, it shows how friendships can be different depending on your financial status.

comments.raw_comment: This graph demonstrates the various statistics of a group of people ages 25 to 44 on the topic of where they have made their friends.  The main thing that stands out is how those with higher income levels are more likely to meet their friends in college in comparison to the average.  People with higher incomes typically have jobs that require college degrees so this makes sense.  On the other end of the spectrum, lower income individuals are more likely to meet their friends in their neighborhood compared to others.  They are not likely to meet friends at college.  This is most likely because those with lower income jobs may not need a college degree.  Those who met friends in work or at high school have relatively the same numbers that are close to the average.  I wonder what these graphs would look like if an older group of individuals was asked this question.  I also wonder, although they did not ask specifics, what demographics make up a majority of these groups.  This relates to me and my community because it is important to have a known area where one can find individuals they can be friends with and relate to.  I would entitle this graph: "Friends In Different Places."

This graph's scale presents additional information not seen in the others; the top end of collegiate friend-makers are 2.4x the national average, significantly higher than the next highest proportion, low income people in the neighborhood. One interpretation of this data is that the highest earners in our society exclusively draw social connections from the elite institutions they attend. The social effect of this phenomenon is most certainly noticeable in our society, where wealthy people stay insulated within themselves, and as the graph shows, rarely interact with those in their neighborhood.
2. I wonder if there is a cause and effect relationship between these studied variables. Are wealthy people more likely to have become wealthy if they made more friends in college?
3. It's interesting that high school is the most even time for friend development as there is generally limited variation across the income spectrum. It's apparently a great environment for interclass interaction and bonding. That's got to be good for our communities.

comments.raw_comment: High income people are much more likely to make friends in college, while low income people are much more likely to make friends in their community. People of all incomes seem fairly equally likely to make friends in high school, as well as the likelihood of making friends at work being fairly distributed, with it being somewhat more likely for middle-income people. I wonder why friendships from high school are so evenly distributed. Maybe it's because of our country's system of free education through 12th grade, while the reason richer people are more likely to have friends from college is because they're more likely to be able to afford going to college at all. Though that begs the question of why are rich people so much less likely to make friends in their communities? They have houses. They have neighborhoods. Do higher income people spend too much time with work to participate in community socialization? No, because if that were the case, rich people should be more likely to have friends from work, which they aren't. Strange. I wonder about the reasons for these differences in friendships because I'm not sure what income my future will lead me to. Will a certain path cause me to develop friendships with certain people less easily? The graph doesn't make clear why, but it looks likely that if I manage to become wealthy, I may not have a good relationship with my community members. Headline: "Wealthy more likely to make friends in college, less so in neighborhoods."

However, I also noticed that while in your neighborhood people tend to make more friends if you have a lower income and in college people tend to make more friends if they have a higher salary.

This is relevant to me and my neighborhood because it's fascinating to observe statistically where people form friendships. However, I also realize that I don't necessarily hang out with people who make more money than I do, and that those people frequently hang out with those same people.

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice? 
I noticed that the graphs for making friends in high school and at work are similarly centered around the 50th percentile, whereas college and neighborhood friends are skewed to the left and right, accordingly.

What do you wonder?
I wonder why work and high school are the two similar ones, whereas the neighborhood category is so dramatically skewed right. I understand why college is skewed left (because only higher-income people can easily afford college) but I don't think the differences between high school, neighborhood, and work are all that obvious, even though the graphs are.

How does this relate to you and your community?
The graphs are somewhat consistent with what I've experiences firsthand, and who I know are people's closest friends and where they met, which is interesting. However, looking at these graphs makes me want to break the pattern in my own community by making friends from all of these categories.

comments.raw_comment: What I take from this graph is that the proportion of friends made from high school or work settings is approximately equal between lower and higher incomes. This makes sense because almost the entire population would be engaged in high school and work environments. However, when it comes to college, there is a strong correlation between higher income and friends made in college; this makes sense because generally, careers stemming from a college education have higher incomes, and therefore those with higher incomes would have likely gone to college, and consequently made more friends in college. When it comes to neighborhoods, there is a strong correlation between lower incomes and making friends. This also makes sense because those who have higher incomes are less likely to live in communal neighborhoods, and therefore are less likely to make friends within a neighborhood. This graph is, as a gestalt, commenting on the fact that everyone makes friends in their own group, more likely or unlikely based on the fact that lower incomes are correlated with neighborhood living, and higher incomes are correlated with college and higher education. I would name this graph “Everyone Has Friends Somewhere”

1) I noticed that in high school, the amount of friends one may have tends to stay the same regardless of their income. However, in college there seems to be a connection between income and the amount of friends one has. There is a 2.4% increase when it comes to having more friends as long as their income also increases. Similarly to the increase, there is a 0.3% decrease in friends for those who have a smaller source of income. At work, making friends is similar to that of highschool with only the tiniest difference of income. While there is this difference, it does not have a significant impact on making friends. Alongside this, the bar representing those who make friends in their neighborhood seems to be skewed to the right as the likelihood of making friends is opposite to that of college.

2) I wonder why people let income influence whether they want to have friends or not. Why is it that friends come and go based directly on income in college? I also wonder what these graphs might look like in other countries where there are more influences. 

3) This relates to me and my community since we come from a pretty low-income area. Our town isn't as big either, which allows so many of us to start off with friends that may follow us into college since we've grown up with them. As a soon to be senior, I may see the difference once I enter college as students may only want to be friends with those of higher wealth classes.

4) "There's Been an Influx: in Friends or Income?"

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed and found it interesting that people who make friends in college tend to be those with high-income (the college graph is skewed left as most people are towards the higher-income level) while those who make their friends from the neighborhood they live in tend to be of lower-income (the neighborhood graph is skewed right as more people are in the lower-incomes). As far as people who make friends in high school and at work, both seem to generally be split between all incomes, with just slightly more being in the middle-incomes (both graphs are fairly uniform, especially high school).
I wonder why making friends in college and making friends in one’s neighborhood are more frequent in the high-income side and low-income side respectively, while for making friends in high school and work, it is fairly split between the classes. If I had to guess, it would be because just about everyone, regardless of income, makes similar relationships and bonds in high school and at their workplace, which is not true in one’s neighborhood or college environment. 
These graphs relate to my community as I live where there are people of a variety of high, middle, and low incomes. Therefore, it is very interesting and relevant to see where each of these groups typically make most of their friends. Also, being in high school, it is interesting to see how a practically equal amount of all incomes make friends at this point in their life. 
Does Your Income Impact Where You Meet Your Friends?

I notice that the graph related to high school is symmetrical, meaning there is little correlation between income and making friends in that area, while in college, there is a right skew showing that high-income people are far more likely to gain friends in college, while in the neighborhood, there is a left skew showing the opposite in that area. This shows that those who are richer tend to make friends in areas where strangers may be present, and lower-income people tend to make more friends in areas where people are closer and more familiar. 

I wonder why something like having money can lead to having significantly higher rates of meeting friends in college, but not in the workplace or in high school, which are somewhat similar environments. I wonder what aspect of the neighborhood makes rich people unable to meet friends in that area, to such a low degree. 

In a lower income area, we tend to basically never see people in the higher income category, so being able to relate or make friends with people like that in our area would be nearly impossible, and as I am about to enter college as a high school senior, I may notice it more difficult to find friends when the more wealthy statically have an advantage over me in that department.  

How Money Really Can Buy Happiness: Where the Most Wealthy Make the Most Friends.

comments.raw_comment:
1. It seems as though income disparity shines most brightly in places where not all tax brackets will be represented equally. Take the college graph, the clearest indicator of a correlation between wealth and the ability to make friends. First and foremost, lower-income families and children from those families don't have access to college, but that's relatively clear and obvious. What isn't so obvious is the fact that those few low-income children who do have the chance to go to college might a. have to work a job in order to pay their tuition or b. they're hyper-aware of the opportunity college presents and they want to make the best of it. 

2. What questions is this supposed to raise? We know there's a huge educational schism between the wealthy and the poor, so what can be done to not only bridge the gap educationally but also make the experiences of those low-income students more beneficial from a social standpoint.

3.  I'm fortunate enough to go to a really fantastic school with incredible people and teachers surrounding me every day, but I've never taken any time to consider the effects that come from a different socioeconomic class that the majority of students in the school come from might mean socially. I understand that the data references both high school and college, but I'm curious to see if there's a divide in that high school data between public and private high schools. 

4. A Friendly Investment: The Cost of Friendship

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I've seen that there are different links between friends and income; the lower your income, the more friends you make, and high school has the fewest friends made.

What do you wonder?
I'm curious why those with lower wages are less likely to establish acquaintances at work. I would assume that people who work earn more money and make more friends than those who live in their neighborhood. I also wonder why folks in their neighborhood earn so much less than everyone else.

How does this relate to you and your community?
The influence this has on my community and myself is that it will inform me how many friends I will make in various aspects of my life, as well as how much money I and they will make. People in our community have friends from our neighborhood and high school, and despite the fact that most of us go to college, our entire family resides in town, so we are always connected and return to town.

What’s going on in this graph?
"Can Money Bring Connection?"

1.  People with higher incomes seem to make more friends with strangers at more social events like college and work. People with lower incomes tend to make friends with people who are in similar situations and with whom they are more familiar, such as in their neighborhoods. Middle-income people make the most friends in high school.

2.  I'm curious if higher-income people make more friends in college because they not only have more opportunities to attend college, but it's also more common for everyone in richer households to attend college, whereas low-income people have many more first-generation students and other financial concerns. It may also be more important to connect with other privileged people as part of networking. Is this a case of the rich getting richer?

3.  This is relevant to my community because I live in a predominantly low-income area, and the charts make sense. People in our community have friends from our neighborhood and high school, and even though most of us go to college, our entire family lives in town, so we are always connected and return to town.

4. "FRIENDS BASED ON INCOME"
